label: Scatterplot Analysis
overview: Scatterplots display the relationship between two quantitative variables. SAT questions ask you to identify the direction (positive/negative) and strength of association, interpret the line of best fit (slope and y-intercept in context), read predicted values, identify outliers, and distinguish correlation from causation.

keyFormulas.name: Slope interpretation
keyFormulas.latex: m = \text{change in } y \text{ per unit increase in } x

workedExamples.problem: A line of best fit for a scatterplot of study hours (x) vs test score (y) is ŷ = 5x + 50. Interpret the slope and predict the score for 8 hours of study.

steps.title: Interpret the slope
steps.content: Slope = 5 means: for each additional hour of study, the predicted test score increases by 5 points.

steps.title: Interpret the y-intercept
steps.content: y-intercept = 50 means: a student who studies 0 hours is predicted to score 50.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing correlation with causation — 'more study causes higher scores'
commonMistakes.fix: A scatterplot shows association, not causation. Two variables can be correlated due to a third hidden variable or by coincidence.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reading the y-intercept as the slope, or vice versa
commonMistakes.fix: Slope (m) is the coefficient of x — the rate of change. Y-intercept (b) is the value when x = 0. In ŷ = 5x + 50, slope is 5, y-intercept is 50.

quickTip: When interpreting the line of best fit in context, always reference the actual units of x and y in your description. 'For each additional [x-unit], y increases/decreases by [slope] [y-units]' is the template.
